title: Inside Azure innovations with Mark Russinovich | BRK226

segments.text: Mark Russinovich: Let's try that again.
Good morning, everybody.
All: Good morning.
Mark Russinovich: How's Build going?
Good? [ Cheers ]
Well, welcome to Inside Azure Innovations.
My name is Mark Russinovich.
I'm the CTO and Deputy CISO for Azure.
How many people have been to a previous innovations talk?
So, quite a few of you.
It's great to see you back.
For those of you that haven't come, this is a talk
where I cover innovations across the spectrum of everything
in the Azure infrastructure, from data centers all the way
to cybersecurity and the cyber systems that we've got
under development in Azure.
One of the notes that I make about this is
that I'm showing you things, in some cases,
that haven't shipped yet, some things that we're working on,
some things that maybe have just shipped.
For things that haven't shipped,
they might not necessarily ever ship or ship in the same kind
of view that you see me present them at.
So that's just a caveat and takeaway.
But I thought it's fun to give you an under-the-hood look
at what we're doing and what powers the infrastructure
of Azure and Azure innovation.
So let's start with infrastructure.
And you've seen these pictures of the Fairwater data centers.
And this kind of sets a framework
for a lot of the innovation that I'm going to be showing here,
which is innovation powering AI, specifically the co-design
of AI data centers, the core infrastructure, and the software
that runs on top of it.
I had a really awesome experience in November.
I got to go visit Fairwater in Atlanta.
These are Fairwater in Wisconsin, Fairwater in Atlanta.
The Atlanta site is on the right.
And I got to go in to it,
and I thought I'd show you a quick video tour of it,
just a few seconds of me walking through it.
And I don't know why that didn't play.
Maybe I need to hit the play button up here.
So this is me looking like Builder Bob walking through.
That's because it's under construction.
It's kind of continuously under construction.
This is the network cabling that connects the top floor
servers and the bottom floor servers that goes
up through trunks there, you can see.
There's enough cabling to wrap the earth four times
in one of these.
Those are liquid cooling cables being laid there initially
so that servers can be dropped in.
And you can see, we got to see one of these servers
on the sled being racked.
These are the cables on the back,
the InfiniBand and Ethernet cables.
And then you can see this is a brake fix that we got to watch.
This is the liquid cooling into the back of the racks.
And then I saw this on the tour.
The group had gone ahead of me.
I saw a plug and I plugged it in.
[ Laughter ]
Because it's like, what's this?
Shouldn't be hanging like that.
And Scott Guthrie got a text literally a few minutes later
saying it looks like we've already powered on Power Cell 3.
We didn't expect that.
I wanted to take credit,
but I thought maybe I best shouldn't for that.
[ Laughter ]
But inside the data centers themselves,
we've got the servers, of course.
And one of the innovations that we've been developing
in our servers is something called Azure Boost.
Azure Boost is aimed at offloading a lot
of the processing of the data paths for storage
and networking off the main server CPUs.
And it does this with an offload card.
We move the data planes off onto that offload card.
We power them with DPUs.
We've got cores on there as well,
where we put our agent tree.
So we get the agents off the server as well,
and this lets the workload have most of the control
over what's going on on the server.
This Azure Boost card looks like this.
This is the latest generation of Azure Boost card
that we've started to deploy in our data centers.
Here's an actual version of it right here.
And what you can see there, there's little black squares
around the middle are D-RAM.
And then the middle is where the SOC is.
That's where the ARM cores and the DPU and FPGA are located.
That's where the data plane gets processed and the agents run.
Now some of the stats for Azure Boost are pretty staggering.
You can see here, just in last year,
since the previous generation of Azure Boost that I showed
at last Build, we've gone
to 20 gigabytes per second of remote storage.
And that's an increase, you can see there, of 1.4.
We've gone to 1 million IOPS for remote storage,
and on local storage, 36 gigabytes per second,
this is to local NVMe, and 6.6 million IOPS
through Azure Boost NVMe offload storage acceleration.
And then for networking,
we've gone to 400 gigabits from 200 gigabits.
So those were two network ports that you saw there on the card,
200 gigabits each, and 400k connections per second,
it supports.
Those two ports mean that they can go
to two top-of-rack router switches, so that means
that we can service top-of-rack routers, or if one fails,
we don't lose complete connectivity to the server.
And it also means
that sub-second servicing is possible now on those tours
with sub-second impact
to the workloads running on those servers.
We've been deploying this for several years now,
and we're over 30% of the fleet is now Azure Boost enabled.
Every single server gets an Azure Boost in it.
And then one of the cool innovations that I'll show you
in a little bit is that we support
guest virtual machine RDMA.
So this is basically memory to memory transfers,
bypassing the networking stacks,
because Azure Boost is facilitating that transport.
One of the things
that I mentioned is we get the management services off the
server, and we put them on the Azure Boost card.
And that lets us have Bare Metal instances.
We've introduced Bare Metal instances
to unlimited access,
specifically for OpenAI
and OpenAI's use of that Fairwater data center.
So the servers in the data center, the GPU servers,
are Bare Metal instances.
And I thought I'd show you just a quick demo
of Bare Metal instances, which are going to be coming
as a general purpose offering sometime in the near future.
But here, you can see we've got a metal instance, ND144 v6.
You can see here we're going to get the IP address,
and then we're going to SSH into it and actually see
that it is a Bare Metal server, because we're going to look
to see if virtualization services are running,
and they're not.
And then we're going to look at the PCI bus using LSPCI.
And you can see we get lots of devices.
We're going to scroll to the top,
and you can see there's a PCI bridge,
and then you can see the eight Ethernet controllers
that are connected
to the Mellanox RDMA-capable network adapters
that are attached to that for the backend network
that those GPUs talk through to each other.
Now what do they talk?
What transport do they talk?
We switched to Ethernet from InfiniBand, actually,
in those Fairwater data centers.
And instead of using RoCE, which is RDMA over converged Ethernet,
we've developed, with OpenAI and now a growing consortium
of partners that are collaborating with us,
a new networking protocol called Multipath Reliable Connection,
or MRC.
And the reason that we developed MRC is that when you talk
about connecting 100,000 GPUs together,
that's an incredible amount of network fabric
that those packets are going across from all of those GPUs.
If you have any congestion or any failure
on a synchronous training job of that size, you're going
to lose a ton of work.
You're going to have to go back to a checkpoint,
restart the training job from where it left off.
So MRC is designed to be resilient in the face
of these congestion issues or failures
because it sprays the packets
across independent network domains called planes.
And therefore, when a link gets dropped,
the spraying just happens and rebalances to the planes
that remain available.
And I'll show you a quick demo of that
in action by showing you here.
What we're going to see is that I've got two servers talking
to each other over four switches.
They're sending 4 gigabyte payloads to each other.
These 4 gigabytes are going to be packet sprayed across these.
And you can see we're getting roughly 95 gigabytes per second,
and that's because we're spraying these
across eight planes with 12 gigabits.
So that comes out to 12 gigabytes per plane.
And this is the aggregate bandwidth that we're seeing,
which is 95 gigabytes per second.
This is what we're going to watch, because we want
to maintain 95 gigabits per second there, which is our goal.
We see four switches.
You can see how much bandwidth
is being spread across the switches.
There's actually two switches at this bandwidth here
that you don't see, so this is 12, two 24s,
and one 36, adding up to 95.
And now we're going to go kill one of those switches.
We're going to drop it off of the sending server.
So what it's going to do is now rebalance the spraying
across the remaining three switches.
And our goal is to not see any drop in network bandwidth.
And, of course, that's exactly what we get.
You can see 95-ish gigabits per second.
And if we go take a look at the traffic over the switches,
you can see that one of them went to zero,
and then the other one went up to 36 gigabits per second
to compensate for that.
So MRC is what allows us to run these massive training jobs
and has now become the industry standard
for large network topologies.
Now I mentioned RDMA a few times.
And what I was showing you was MRC, which is what Open AI uses
for their training jobs.
And they're doing RDMA, of course, between the servers
in those training jobs.
But what we want to introduce is
to more general-purpose workloads RDMA
through virtual machines.
Now when you talk between one VM and another VM
through Azure Boost, they could be on different servers,
you're going through these networking stacks.
The application talks to TCP/IP, which talks to our MANA driver,
the Microsoft Accelerated Network Adapter driver,
which is the Azure Boost network adapter driver,
and then it goes back up.
And there's a lot of memory copy operations and a lot
of synchronization happening through that.
With RDMA, you bypass all that.
So the application maps memories basically in the remote system,
can drop data right into its own local presentation of that,
and Azure Boost takes care of sending that and dropping it
in the memory on the other side.
And this completely eliminates a lot of that synchronization
as well as the memory copies and all that software path
that you get through those networking stack.
So I'm going to show you a demo of virtual machine
to virtual machine RDMA over Azure Boost.
The scenario here is common in AI workloads,
where you're doing inference.
And inference, you can break up into two parts:
prefill and decode.
Prefill is taking your prompt and then getting the tokens
from that prompt and the KV cache populated
from that prompt.
And then decode starts to generate new tokens based off
of that system of that prompt.
So it's efficient and now common to split those
into different server pools, so one pool for prefill,
one pool for decode, because they both have different
constraints when it comes to memory and compute.
So here, we're going to start this demo
of... RDMA.
So first, we're going to look at the performance
over the TCP/IP stack.
So here's the pre-filler server using TCP/IP.
Here's the decoder server, also using TCP/IP,
the way we're launching it.
And then we're going to go run this vLLM benchmark
that does this prefill decode load between those two servers.
And then we're going to go take a look at our RDMA stats,
which is in the bottom right.
And you're going to see that they don't change
as this workload runs, there's 460 send requests.
Just keep your eye on that one.
But then if you take a look at the performance,
the token throughput, which is what we really want,
is about 3,400.
The median time to first token, which is another important stat
for inference, is 123,000.
But when we switch over to RDMA and use the MANA link for that,
you can see there's the F1 Verbs Device Name as MANA 0.
We do the same thing on the decode server, MANA 0.
And then let's go take a look at the stats, and you can see 460,
but this is going to change now,
because we're running the RDMA test.
And it changed to 506 because we've sent a whole lot
of packets now over to RDMA.
And then we've almost doubled the throughput to 7637.
And then you can see our mean time to first token has dropped
to just 47,000 milliseconds.
So that's the performance benefit of RDMA
that we're deploying and using
in our inference clusters behind Foundry, powered by Azure Boost.
Okay, so let's take a look at our core now.
So that's kind of Fairwater infrastructure and some
of the networking behind it.
Let's go take a look at the core.
And this is one of the sections that I get very excited about,
because the future is serverless.
And I've been saying this for a long time.
If you've come to previous Inside Azure Innovation talks,
even going back 10 years,
I've been saying serverless is the future.
Well, serverless as the future is really arriving now
with Azure Container Instances, which Azure Container instances,
the idea here is that we've got --
typically, when it comes to containers,
you think about containers the way they started,
which is process isolated containers.
So they're using the operating system primitives to try
to keep them separate from each other.
But there's a problem with that.
We don't consider a process or user mode kernel
as a security boundary in Azure.
We only consider virtualization with a very tight connection
between -- small connection between the server and the host
to be a security boundary in Azure.
So with Azure Container Instances,
we isolate those containers with Hyper-V.
And this is nested hypervisor here inside
a virtual machine with the containers on them.
One of the things I'm going to show you in a little bit
is where we're going with this, which is direct virtualization.
So I'll save a description of that.
But what I want to show you is we're making a ton of progress
in adopting Azure Container Instances throughout all
of not just Azure, but Microsoft services.
I'm sure that if you take a look at this,
you can see some service that you've been using,
which means you're indirectly using Azure Container Instances,
whether, for example, GitHub Actions is now running
on Azure Container Instances.
You can see Python and Excel
running on Azure Container Instances.
Horizon DB, which you might have gone to sessions about
here at Build, running on Azure Container Instances.
So one of the things that we've been doing is trying
to make Container Instances more efficient
and also support more scenarios and make it
so that you never need to do process isolation.
One of those is taking out the virtualization overhead.
And this is what we call direct virtualization,
is putting the containers right on the servers as peers
to the management's virtual machine.
We call this the parent partition
or Layer 1 virtualization host.
And these are Layer 2 virtualization hosts,
or child VMs, that are simply hosting
individual containers, or pods.
And this gives us that strong hostile multi-tenant isolation
for container instances.
Now one of the other Azure Container Instances of cells now
runs on top of 01 virtualization or direct virtualization,
where we're migrating our entire fleet
over to direct virtualization.
This will probably take a year or two
to migrate the whole fleet, but this is something that is going
to give us a lot of performance and efficiency benefits.
Now we want to make containers have all
of the same capabilities of virtual machines,
all of the same abilities
to attach network devices and storage devices.
One of the benefits you get out of a virtual machine today
on any hyperscaler, including Azure, is minimal downtime
when the server needs to be serviced
or the server is going unhealthy,
and we recognize that ahead of time.
And that is with live migration.
What's been missing
with containers is support for live migration.
So I want to show you the first public demo
of Container Live Migration in Azure here,
where we can take a bunch of containers and move them
from one server over to another server.
So here I've got a container that's running
on one pool of servers.
And here's another pool of servers over here
that we're going to migrate it to.
So this is our live migration for container instances.
You can see this is still under development,
which is why we're using these command lines here.
And we've got this running over on Dev Box 6, Server Dev 6.
And we've got this container workload, it's simply spitting
out a tick every second.
You can see we're up to Tick 695.
And the migration now has kicked in
and that container is no longer running on that server,
which is why that stopped.
Now if we go over and take a look at the other server,
it's migrated to, Dev 1,
and we look at what's running in it.
You can see that there's our Hello World there.
And if we go take a look at what's running inside of that,
you can see there is the file
that it's been dropping those ticks into.
We're already way way up to 755.
So let's go take a look and make sure that 695 was in there,
and we didn't have any kind of gap.
So we're going to go to a CAT, scroll back up.
And there it is, 695 right there.
So no gap at all.
So container live migrating from one server to another on top
of Azure Container Instance.
By the way, feel free to clap at any time.
[ Applause ]
All right.
Let's switch over to talking a little bit about AI.
I know that there's AI fatigue,
but I think we're doing some cool stuff
with AI that I'd like to share with you.
And one of those is talking a little bit about what powers all
of Microsoft's own inference and own training,
and that's a system called Manifold.
Manifold's idea is to treat all our pool of GPUs as one pool
to do priority-based deployments of workloads
to understand the topologies of AI-based inference
and training workloads to most efficiently use
that GPU capacity
and to also abstract the underlying hardware.
You can see that it supports ASICS,
it supports GPUs, FPGAs, and even CPUs.
And more and more, we have models that consist
of CPU portions of the model and GPU portions of the model,
including models that actually have mini models inside of them,
like they might have an embedding model within them.
They might have a visual large language model embedded
within them, if they're a multimodal model.
And so these topologies are getting more complicated.
Now what we want to do is bring this power
of Azure container instances in this isolation to workloads
like this on top of direct virtualization,
where we can put CPU containers inside
of its own Hyper-V isolated container
and the AI model components, those containers,
in their own separate ones too, so they don't interfere
with each other, and they get direct access
to hardware at the same time.
And this is a benefit of direct virtualization is we can assign
the GPU to a virtual machine.
That virtual machine can then create a sub-virtual machine,
one of these L2s, and then give the GPUs that it's got
over to that container.
And then it has direct access to that hardware.
So let me show you this demo of Manifold.
And what we're going to see here is if I get the nodes
in this cluster, we're going to go take a look at one
of those nodes and get the pods in the node.
And there's one pod in there, which is Llama 4 server.
And there's another one, which is a metrics server.
One of them is a GPU-based one, one is a CPU-based one.
When we go take a look inside the pod that's got the GPU,
the Llama model in it, you can see it's got
the GPUs visible to it
It's got a whole bunch of RAM visible to it.
And it's got a whole bunch of processors assigned to it.
And you can see the Nvidia SMI command shows us
that it actually has those GPUs available to it.
When we go take a look at the CPU pod sitting right next to it
on the same server, you can see that it's got almost no memory.
It's only got two processors.
And it's got no GPUs attached to it.
And just to prove to you it works,
we're going to go take a look at this cat video and send this
for inference to that GPU pod sitting there with direct access
to GPUs, the Llama 4 Maverick model there,
and then successfully do an inference there.
The point being proven here
that we've got CPU pods completely isolated
from GPU pods directly attached to the physical server hardware
because of direct virtualization.
[ Applause ]
Now we're also not just optimizing the compute.
We're also optimizing the way that inference works in terms
of KV caches, which is --
the KV cache is effectively the state of the LLM.
And you can't do decoding efficiently
without having a KV cache which represents the processing
of all the previous tokens in the prompt.
When you interact with an LLM, you do so typically using turns.
And so you might have Turn 1,
where you just have a system prompt.
Let's say you're doing a PR diff
because you're doing development.
And you engage in an interaction with Copilot on that PR diff.
And what that means is
that you're extending the prompt effectively,
your specific prompt.
In an ideal case, you don't just want to cache the system prompt.
And this is what a lot of AI frameworks
let you do is they say, hey,
cache this for me, and then I'm not going to have
to pay the cost for decoding this again or prefilling it.
But what you really want is the whole thing to be cached,
so that if your workload moves, your inference moves from one GP
to another, one server to another,
that you're not repaying this price.
And we can only do this if we've got a cache
that sits all the way behind all of the servers.
So this is something that we've got coming
out in preview now called Azure Context Cache.
The idea here is that Azure Context Cache, behind it,
has a storage account.
And that storage account is where we're caching the KV state
for all of the inference requests.
So regardless of what server they go to,
if the prompt is not there, the KV isn't there, we can look it
up in the cache and fetch it in and not have to decode
that again, saving time and money.
So let's go take a look at that Azure Context Cache in action.
So here, we're sending, concurrency level one,
we're sending a bunch of queries into the system,
all with the same system prompt.
And you can see that we had all of those cached.
The cache hit rate was 81%,
because after the first request goes to the server,
the next one is likely gonna have
that system prompt already cached in it.
But when we do a concurrency level of 10, they're going
to get sprayed across servers,
and our cache hit rate actually goes
down because now sometimes a request is landing on a server
without the system prompt.
So a lot of systems have you set this cache key unique to try
to pin a conversation on a particular server, an endpoint.
The hit rate actually drops there
because every conversation gets mapped
to a different server intentionally
where the system prompt might not have already shown up.
So the first hit there is always --
the first query there is always going to be a miss.
But when we set the prompt cache,
you can see that the prompt cache rate,
hit rate is going to go up.
Where did the demo go here?
Went up to 96% with the remote cache here;
96.2% is the hit rate here.
And that's because no matter which server the query lands on,
the prompt is -- the KV cache for that prompt is going
to be fetched from remote cache if it wasn't there.
So transparently, behind the scenes,
this prompt cache using Azure storage to go and spread
out the KV cache across the servers,
effectively making the servers have a pool cache rather
than individual server-based caches, which is going
to improve hit rate, which is going to save money,
so you're not having to pay for the prefill
on those system caches every time you have a miss.
All right.
So let's take a look at the next cool innovation.
And I've got a -- it's like an ACI-themed talk,
because this is one of the cool things about ACI.
When you talk about containers, you're talking
about layers and images.
When you talk about virtual machines, you're talking
about full-blown virtual machine images.
Now, when you talk about container sandboxes,
you're typically talking about something that is very bespoke,
kind of a custom image, and it's very small and lightweight.
And this is what you want to be extremely fast.
Now one of the ways to get a fast startup
for a container image, which you want with these for these agents
to be able to say, "I'm going to go write a Python script
and run it, I'm going to go create a little HTML site
and iterate on it," is you want the startup to be
close to instantaneous.
When it comes to containers, you can get startup times
in the five, 20-second range, depending on what the OS is.
But we want literally thousands of these things to be able
to start simultaneously and to start very quickly off
of the same base image.
The way we do that is with memory snapshotting.
So we actually start the container, snapshot its memory,
and then if you get a request for the same container,
we simply map the memory, and we skip all the initialization
and map it right into a running container box.
So let me show you one of, I think, my favorite demo of this,
which is, how would you like to see 10,000 container
sandboxes launch?
Okay, because if the answer is yes,
that's the rest of the session. [ Laughter ]
I'm just kidding, no, I'm just kidding.
What I'm going to show you is
that we can do this incredibly quickly.
So I've got 10 workers launching 1,000
of these container sandboxes each.
And we've got a little animation to show you the progress
of those launches here.
So here we go.
Create 10 worker pods.
Here we go.
So each one is going to add 1,000.
This represents 1,000.
You can see them launching.
A few down here left.
Boom done.
10,000 container sandboxes.
[ Applause ]
Average container sandbox launch time, two seconds.
So not just speed, but scale at the same time.
So this is, like I said, one of the really cool demos.
And so you're going to see the agent sandboxing land on top
of Azure Container Instance.
All right.
Let's go into our last section now and talk about,
or second to last section,
and talk a little bit about security.
And one of the exciting things for me
about security is the evolution
of something called confidential computing.
How many people have heard of confidential computing?
So, quite a few of you.
For those of you that haven't heard of confidential computing,
the easiest way to think about it is in the context
of how your data gets protected.
And for a long time now,
everybody encrypts their network traffic.
Over the last 20 years or so, it went from every now
and then you'd run into a site with SSL.
And now every single site,
every single network connection has to have TLS on it.
Then, the other part
of protecting is while it's at rest.
And this is where it's stored on disk.
You want to have that encrypted, too,
so if the storage gets accessed outside of the protection
of the logical protections of the workload on top of it,
that the data is useless.
And we not only have now in cloud.
We started with node data encryption at rest.
And now we've got server-side encryption.
We also have customer managed key,
where you can bring your own encryption
and have double layered encryption of data at rest.
But what's been missing largely is protecting the data while
it's in use, because when that data gets decrypted
on the server or pulled off the disk in clear text, it's sitting
in there on the server, maybe inside of a virtual machine,
but still in the server environment.
And what can access that data includes everything
from the hypervisor to the admins to the host software
to a malicious hacker that might penetrate the infrastructure.
All of those can get access.
And even in your own applications,
you want to keep maybe your own operators away from that data
and only have the compute that needs to have access
to that data have access to that data.
That is confidential computing.
Now one aspect of confidential computing
that is not just this protection of that data
in a hardware enclave,
where none of those things can get inside of it,
is that the hardware also can measure what's inside
the enclave.
And that measurement is called an attestation.
And some code inside that enclave can ask the hardware
for a quote, which is the attestation,
present it to a relying party,
which is typically a key management service
that has a policy on it that says only release this key
to an enclave of this hardware type
with the security version number on it
with this configuration of code.
And at that point, the key gets released.
It's encrypted to the enclave, the code in the enclave.
The code in the enclave decrypts the key and then can start
to process the data in the clear, and everybody knows
that it's being protected with that hardware isolation.
That is confidential computing.
We've been working on enabling confidential computing in Azure
for over a decade, starting with Intel SGX servers
in the data center, and now virtual machines from AMD
and Intel in the data center.
And our portfolio is the largest of any hyperscaler when it comes
to confidential computing services,
confidential computing container offerings
like confidential containers on ACI,
as well as the hardware infrastructure underneath it.
I talked before about live migration.
And live migration is one of those things that allows us
to run the fleet efficiently, because we can move workloads
around to reduce fragmentation.
We can also make customer workloads more reliable
because we can move them if we see a server is going to fail.
We can also move them around if we need
to service a host in an impactful way.
And that means that the customer's workload is not
as impacted by that servicing operation.
It is a fundamental requirement of a hyperscale cloud
to have live migration.
And this has unfortunately been one of the missing gaps
in confidential computing offerings is lack
of live migration.
So we've been working deeply with Intel
on confidential live migration.
And the way that works is you have a confidential virtual
machine here on one server.
We've got something called a migration TD,
which is a partition, effectively.
Think of it as a confidential partition that is also measured
as part of the virtual machine's measurement
and that the receiving side has a policy and the sending side
as a policy that says I will only migrate the contents
of this virtual machine to another server with the MigTD
